paras: The threatened lynching of Sol Butcher took place near Dresden, Tennessee, in the spring of 1903, when a crowd hunted a Black man accused of cutting the Weakley County sheriff while resisting arrest. Butcher escaped, and the local paper predicted he would be lynched if caught. He was later arrested in Illinois, where he fought extradition on the ground that he would be lynched, but Illinois granted Tennessee's requisition after Weakley County officials gave assurances.
The Dresden jail had burned a short time before, and the same column reported that the county court had named a committee to build a replacement costing between $12,000 and $15,000.

According to the Union City Commercial, Butcher, whom it called "a desperate negro," created a disturbance in Dresden on a Monday and fled when the sheriff came after him. The sheriff overtook him, and before he could dismount Butcher cut him on the head and hands with a knife. The sheriff was described as seriously wounded but expected to recover.

Bloodhounds brought from Martin could not follow Butcher's trail, and he was thought to be hiding in thick woods about a mile north of town. "A big crowd is in pursuit," the paper reported, adding that should he be captured "a lynching is almost sure to result."

No capture in Tennessee was reported; the next news of Butcher came from Kentucky and Illinois. In late May, Paducah police arrested a man who matched the description left by a Weakley County deputy, down to scars, facial spots and a deformed hand, but he said he was Amrose McDaniels and had never been in Weakley County, and he was released when word came that the right man had been arrested in Illinois. Telegrams reported that the sheriff himself, by then nearly recovered, had caught Butcher near Carbondale, and that Butcher refused to return without a requisition.

At a hearing in Springfield, Butcher, now charged with assaulting L. D. Dodd with a knife with intent to kill, resisted extradition, alleging that he would be lynched if taken back to Weakley County. Acting Governor Northcott postponed the case to hear from the county, whose judge and other officials sent word that there was "not the slightest danger" of a lynching, and on June 8 he issued a warrant on the Tennessee governor's requisition. No report of Butcher's return to Tennessee, a trial or a lynching was found.

Coverage came entirely from white papers, and no Black-press report of the case was found. The Union City Commercial gave the pursuit a single paragraph under "Incidents at Dresden," beside news of the jail committee, and stated the expected lynching without comment. The Paducah Sun's "Wanted Elsewhere" was mainly about the mistaken arrest in that city.

The extradition hearing reached a wider audience through a Springfield dispatch, printed in the Montgomery Advertiser and the Marshalltown, Iowa, Evening Times-Republican on June 9, which called Butcher "colored" and set his fear of lynching beside the officials' assurance without weighing them.

The papers spell the sheriff's name as Dobbs, Dodds and L. D. Dodd. The date of the cutting is also uncertain, since the Commercial's item says only "Monday" and appears in a column that calls the jail fire "two weeks ago."

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Sol Butcher
bases: A crowd pursued Butcher after he was accused of cutting the sheriff and the local paper predicted he would be lynched if caught, but no violence against him is reported; he was later arrested in Illinois and extradited (A2, A4, A5).

Only the Union City Commercial reports the pursuing crowd and the expected lynching (A2); the cutting of the sheriff, Butcher's arrest in Illinois and his fear of lynching are confirmed by separate Paducah and Springfield reports (A4, A5).

accounts.label: Local white weekly (Union City Commercial)
accounts.gist: Butcher, 'a desperate negro', created a disturbance, cut the sheriff before he could dismount, and fled to the woods; a big crowd was in pursuit and a lynching was 'almost sure to result' if he were caught.

accounts.label: Butcher's claim at the extradition hearing
accounts.gist: Butcher resisted extradition, alleging he would be lynched if returned to Weakley County.

accounts.label: Weakley County officials
accounts.gist: The county judge and other officials sent word that there was not the slightest danger of Butcher being lynched.

framing.detail: The Union City Commercial ran the item under 'Incidents at Dresden' beside jail-building news, called Butcher 'a desperate negro' and forecast a lynching without comment.
The Paducah Sun's 'Wanted Elsewhere' focused on the mistaken local arrest and the description of scars, facial spots and a deformed hand.
The Springfield wire ('Northcott Honors Requisition') reported Butcher's fear of lynching and the officials' assurance side by side without judging either.

conflicts.note: Likely one man; a March 1903 Union City Commercial report on the Dresden jail fire (A1) also calls the Weakley sheriff 'Sheriff Dodd', which favors Dodd.

versions.value: A lynching 'almost sure to result' if captured (April); Butcher said he would be lynched if returned (June)
Weakley officials: 'not the slightest danger' of lynching

conflicts.note: The officials' assurance came two months after the pursuit and from the side seeking his return.

versions.value: 'Monday' in a column printed Friday, April 10, 1903

conflicts.note: The same column says the jail burned 'two weeks ago'; A1 dates the fire to March 12, so the item may have been written in late March and 'Monday' may be March 23 or 30 rather than April 6.
